data.description: Implement workspace-aware path resolution for riotplan MCP tools so they automatically detect the workspace root and use the plans/ directory instead of defaulting to the MCP server's process.cwd()

data.note: Current behavior: MCP tools use process.cwd() which points to the MCP server's working directory (often user's home directory), not the workspace root
Expected behavior: Tools should detect workspace root (where .code-workspace file exists) and use the plans/ directory within that workspace
Affects all riotplan MCP tools that create directories: idea_create, shaping_start, and any other tools that write to the filesystem

data.constraint: Must work in Cursor workspace contexts (multi-root workspaces)
Should gracefully fall back if no workspace is detected (e.g., when running from CLI)
Must not break existing behavior for users who explicitly pass the directory parameter

data.question: How can MCP tools access Cursor's workspace context? Is there an environment variable or API?
Should we walk up the directory tree looking for .code-workspace files, or use a different detection method?
What if there are multiple plans/ directories in different workspace roots? Which one should be used?

data.note: Current architecture: The MCP server sets `context.workingDirectory` to `process.cwd()` at line 91 of server.ts. This value is then used by `resolveDirectory()` in shared.ts which has a fallback chain: args.path → context.workingDirectory → process.cwd()

The fix point: We need to modify line 91 in server.ts to set workingDirectory to a workspace-aware path instead of process.cwd(). This single change would cascade to all tools through the resolveDirectory() helper.

Scope: 35 instances of process.cwd() across idea.ts, shaping.ts, history.ts, and step.ts tools. However, most use the resolveDirectory() helper, so fixing the context.workingDirectory would handle many cases automatically.

Research finding: This is a known issue in the MCP ecosystem. When MCP servers are launched via uvx/npx, they run in sandboxed environments where process.cwd() returns cache paths (~/.cache/uv/) rather than the workspace directory. There's currently no standardized SDK method to access workspace context.

Potential solution 1: Pass workspace root via environment variable in .cursor/mcp.json configuration. Cursor allows setting env vars per server. We could add RIOTPLAN_WORKSPACE_ROOT and use it if available.

Potential solution 2: Walk up directory tree from process.cwd() looking for workspace markers (.code-workspace, .git, plans/ directory). This would work automatically without configuration but adds filesystem overhead.

Potential solution 3: Hybrid approach - check for RIOTPLAN_WORKSPACE_ROOT env var first, fall back to directory tree walking if not set, finally fall back to process.cwd() for CLI usage. This provides best of both worlds.

data.constraint: Performance: Directory tree walking should be efficient and cached to avoid repeated filesystem operations on every tool call
Security: Must not traverse outside reasonable bounds (e.g., stop at user home directory or filesystem root) to prevent security issues
Backward compatibility: Existing users who pass explicit directory parameters must continue to work without changes

data.note: Answer to Q1: MCP tools can access environment variables via process.env. Cursor's mcp.json allows setting env vars per server. We can leverage this for explicit configuration while also implementing automatic detection.

Answer to Q2: Directory tree walking is the most reliable automatic method. Look for markers in order: .code-workspace file, plans/ directory, .git directory. Stop at user home or filesystem root to prevent unbounded traversal.

Answer to Q3: For multi-root workspaces, prioritize the first workspace root found when walking up from process.cwd(). Users can override with explicit path parameter or RIOTPLAN_WORKSPACE_ROOT env var if they need a specific root.

data.description: Proof of concept for workspace detection logic showing the hybrid approach with env var, directory walking, and fallback

data.note: Implementation strategy: Create a new workspace-utils.ts module with getWorkspaceRoot() function. Modify server.ts line 91 to use getWorkspaceRoot() instead of process.cwd(). Add caching to avoid repeated filesystem operations. Update resolveDirectory() in shared.ts to use the new utility.

data.question: What happens if a user has nested workspaces (e.g., a plans/ directory inside another plans/ directory)? Should we handle this case or document it as unsupported?
Should we add logging/debugging output to help users understand which workspace root was detected? Could be helpful for troubleshooting.

data.note: Benefits: 1) Better UX - tools "just work" without needing to pass paths. 2) Consistency - all tools use the same workspace root. 3) Flexibility - supports both automatic detection and explicit configuration. 4) Backward compatible - existing explicit path parameters still work.

Testing considerations: Need to test scenarios - 1) MCP server in Cursor with workspace, 2) MCP server in Cursor without workspace markers, 3) CLI usage (should still work), 4) Explicit RIOTPLAN_WORKSPACE_ROOT env var, 5) Nested directories, 6) Symlinks

Exploration summary: This idea is well-scoped and feasible. The hybrid approach (env var + auto-detection + fallback) addresses the core problem while maintaining backward compatibility. The POC demonstrates the implementation approach. Main implementation work: 1) Create workspace-utils.ts module, 2) Update server.ts context initialization, 3) Add tests for all scenarios, 4) Update documentation with RIOTPLAN_WORKSPACE_ROOT usage. Estimated complexity: Medium - touches core path resolution but changes are localized.

REVISED APPROACH: Simplified three-tier configuration strategy: 1) RIOTPLAN_PLAN_DIRECTORY env var (highest priority, explicit), 2) riotplan.config.json file with planDirectory setting (project-level config), 3) Auto-detect plans/ directory from workspace root (convenience fallback). This decouples the concerns and gives users clear configuration options.

Benefits of config file approach: 1) Project-portable configuration (checked into git), 2) No need to modify .cursor/mcp.json for each project, 3) Works consistently across different IDEs/environments, 4) Can include other riotplan settings in future, 5) Explicit and discoverable (users can see the config file)

Config file location: Look for riotplan.config.json starting from process.cwd() and walking up the directory tree (similar to how eslint.config.js, tsconfig.json work). Stop at workspace root or filesystem boundaries. This allows config to be at workspace root or in subdirectories.

data.description: Example riotplan.config.json showing project-level configuration for plan directory

data.note: Key insight: By using a config file, we get project-portability. Team members can clone a repo with riotplan.config.json and it "just works" without needing to configure environment variables. The env var remains available for personal overrides or CI/CD scenarios.

Config file discovery: Walk up from process.cwd() looking for riotplan.config.json (same pattern as eslint, prettier, tsconfig). This allows the config to live at workspace root or in subdirectories. Relative paths in config are resolved from the config file's location.

Should we provide a CLI command to initialize the config file? Something like `riotplan init` that creates riotplan.config.json with sensible defaults?

data.description: JSON Schema for riotplan.config.json providing IDE autocomplete and validation

data.note: Comparison to original approach: This is cleaner because: 1) Explicit over implicit - users know exactly where config comes from, 2) No "magic" workspace detection unless explicitly needed (tier 3), 3) Config file is portable and version-controllable, 4) Simpler mental model - just three clear tiers, 5) Future-proof - config file can grow to include other settings without changing the resolution logic.

Implementation changes from original: 1) Remove RIOTPLAN_WORKSPACE_ROOT, replace with RIOTPLAN_PLAN_DIRECTORY, 2) Add config file discovery and parsing logic, 3) Workspace detection becomes tier 3 fallback only, 4) Update all documentation to explain the three-tier system, 5) Consider adding 'riotplan init' command to bootstrap config file.

data.content:
User explaining default behavior context: "It depends on the context. If I'm running RiotPlan in an IDE like Claude Code in VSCode, Cursor, or just straight up VSCode, I likely would want you to look at the workspace that this project is in and find the root directory. For the project I work on, I have multiple folders in a workspace, but my workspace root is usually the same directory that my workspace file is in. That is the directory which usually has a plans/ directory in it, and I usually want you to use that directory.

If I'm running this from the command line, it's very likely that I'm going to be running it within a project that has a plans directory somewhere up the chain. So, for example, let's assume I'm in the terminal and I'm in this directory /Users/tobrien/gitw/kjerneverk/riotplan/src/analysis - well, I know that this is part of the kjerneverk project and if I walk up the chain of directories, I'm going to notice that I have a ./plans directory here /Users/tobrien/gitw/kjerneverk/plans

Now I understand that this is a lot of work, but in this case it would be valid to walk up the path and find the first directory that has a plans subdirectory and assume that this is where I want to put the plan."
data.context: User explaining how plan directory resolution should work in different contexts (IDE vs CLI)
data.speaker: user

data.content:
User on configuration precedence and boundaries: "Another idea which should take precedence over walking up the path to find that plans subdirectory is someone specifically configuring riotplan with either a riotplan.config.json or a .riotplan configuration directory (IMPORTANT NOTE HERE I WANT YOU TO ALLOW FOLKS TO USE DIFFERENT CONFIGURATION APPROACHES)

As far as boundaries go, don't stop. Just keep on going up."

data.speaker: user

data.content:
User on auto-detection and config files: "Don't use Auto-detection based on the presence of Git files, I happen to have a lot of hybrid workspaces that aren't actually workspaces.

Not all projects have to have a riotplan.config.json or a .riotplan. In fact they should rarely have that."
data.context: User clarifying auto-detection approach and config file expectations
data.speaker: user

data.note: Key insight: The resolution strategy should be "walk up until you find a plans/ directory" - this works for both IDE and CLI usage. Example: running from /Users/tobrien/gitw/kjerneverk/riotplan/src/analysis should find /Users/tobrien/gitw/kjerneverk/plans
Important: Config files (riotplan.config.json or .riotplan/) should take PRECEDENCE over auto-detection. Config is explicit intent, auto-detection is convenience.
User wants flexibility: Support BOTH riotplan.config.json (file) AND .riotplan/ (directory) as configuration approaches. Users should be able to choose their preferred style.
No boundaries on directory traversal - keep walking up until filesystem root if needed. Don't stop at home directory or other artificial boundaries.
Don't use .git or package.json as project markers - user has hybrid workspaces that aren't traditional projects. Only look for plans/ directory or explicit config.
Config files should be RARE - most projects won't need them. Auto-detection by finding plans/ directory should handle the common case.

data.description: CardiganTime GitHub repository - comprehensive configuration management library with multi-format support (YAML, JSON, JS, TS), hierarchical discovery, and MCP integration

data.note: CardiganTime features discovered: 1) Multi-format support (YAML, JSON, JS, TS), 2) Hierarchical config discovery (walks up directory tree), 3) Multiple naming conventions (app.config.ext, .app/config.ext, .apprc, etc.), 4) MCP integration built-in, 5) Zod schema validation, 6) Config precedence handling (CLI args > config file > defaults)

CardiganTime already handles hierarchical discovery! We can use its 'enabled' mode (default) to walk up the directory tree looking for config. This means we don't have to implement our own config discovery - CardiganTime does it for us.

CardiganTime naming conventions: riotplan.config.{yaml,json,js,ts}, riotplan.conf.{ext}, .riotplan/config.{ext}, .riotplanrc.{ext}, .riotplanrc. This gives users maximum flexibility in how they configure riotplan.

data.note: DECISION: Use Option A - CardiganTime for tiers 1-2 (env var + config), custom walk-up for tier 3 (finding existing plans/). This ensures normal users can download and use RiotPlan without any configuration setup.
Environment variable support will be added to CardiganTime itself (not just in RiotPlan). This is needed for container implementations and will benefit all CardiganTime users.
Key insight: Configuration should be optional. The walk-up (tier 3) is critical for zero-config experience - users can just start using RiotPlan and it finds their plans/ directory automatically.

Implementation plan: 1) Add env var support to CardiganTime (separate task), 2) Integrate CardiganTime in RiotPlan with Zod schema for planDirectory, 3) Implement custom walk-up function to find existing plans/ directory, 4) Wire up the four-tier resolution in server.ts and resolveDirectory()

Final four-tier hierarchy: 1) RIOTPLAN_PLAN_DIRECTORY env var (via CardiganTime), 2) CardiganTime config file (riotplan.config.*, .riotplan/config.*, etc.), 3) Walk up looking for existing plans/ subdirectory, 4) Fallback to ./plans in current directory
